source.title_on_document: Comparative Study of Generative AI and Traditional Tools for Evaluating Creativity and Efficiency in UI/UX Design

paper_design_summary: In a controlled laboratory experiment, 26 final-year undergraduate students and 18 UI/UX professionals were randomly assigned within expertise category to Galileo AI or Figma to create a Patient Overview screen for a healthcare application (PDF pp. 6-8, printed pp. 929-931, Research Methodology and Procedure). The authors created separate novice and expert datasets, recorded below as separate study entries (PDF p. 8, printed p. 931, Data Preparation and Processing). Two UI/UX design professionals rated the completed screens using the Creative Product Semantic Scale (CPSS); each participant received a creativity score averaging six items on a 5-point Likert scale, while cognitive load and completion time were also measured (PDF p. 8, printed p. 931, Evaluation & Measurement and Data Preparation and Processing).

assignment.what_was_assigned: Use of Galileo AI versus the traditional design tool Figma, randomized separately within the novice and expert participant categories.
assignment.quote: We randomly divided both types of participants into two groups i.e. AI and traditional.

arms.name: AI (Galileo AI)

participants.who: Final-year undergraduate students from a public university in Islamabad, Pakistan, designated as novices. They had foundational design knowledge, Figma proficiency, and prior experience with generative AI design tools, but had not used Galileo AI.
participants.quote: These participants belonged to two categories: 26 senior students (final-year undergraduate students) from a public university in Islamabad, Pakistan, and 18 UI/UX design professionals, each with at least one year of experience in the UI/UX design field.

ai_tool.how_used: Generative UI design: participants used Galileo AI to produce the required healthcare application screen. The tool is described as accepting text prompts or image-based inputs, but the actual prompts and interaction protocol are not specified (PDF p. 6, printed p. 929, Tools; PDF pp. 7-8, printed pp. 930-931, The Split and Phase 2: The Experiment).

task.description: Create a Patient Overview screen for a healthcare application, including a top navigation bar, patient information card, health summary, and upcoming appointments. Both arms received the same design brief (PDF p. 8, printed p. 931, Written Design Brief).

eligibility.reason: The text explicitly states random assignment to Galileo AI or Figma within both expertise categories (PDF p. 7, printed p. 930, The Split), in a controlled laboratory setting (PDF p. 6, printed p. 929, Research Methodology). Only 44 people participated across the separate novice (26; 13 per arm) and expert (18; 9 per arm) datasets (PDF p. 7, Participant Recruitment and The Split); the analyzed counts are confirmed by the creativity tables (PDF p. 12, printed p. 935, Tables 8 and 10). Both datasets, and even their combined total, are below the 50-person threshold. Creativity was scored on completed design screens by UI/UX professionals using CPSS (PDF p. 8, printed p. 931, Rating Design Screens using CPSS and Data Preparation and Processing). This is a small randomized experiment excluded from the core dataset, with no applicable context class.

one_line_finding: Galileo AI yielded lower expert-rated CPSS creativity than Figma among novices (M = 3.269 vs. 3.939; p = 0.023) and professionals (M = 3.367 vs. 4.167; p = 0.001) (PDF p. 12, printed p. 935, Tables 8-11).
